titlePl: Matura PR: Sport — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Sport — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Sport na maturę rozszerzoną: dyscypliny, obiekty, zawody, trening i problemy sportu. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended-level Sport vocabulary for the Polish Matura: disciplines, venues, events, training and sporting issues. ENG–PL flashcards.

items.definitionEn: track and field sports such as running, jumping and throwing
items.example: School sports day includes athletics events from the 100 metres to the shot put.

items.definitionEn: a sport of exercises on the floor and apparatus that need strength, balance and control
items.example: Gymnastics training at this club starts at six in the morning.

items.definitionEn: combat sports such as judo, karate or taekwondo
items.example: She took up martial arts after a self-defence course at school.

items.definitionEn: sports with a high level of danger or adrenaline, such as climbing or rafting
items.example: Insurers charge more if you regularly do extreme sports.

items.definitionEn: competitive racing in cars, motorbikes or similar vehicles
items.example: Motorsport on public roads is illegal without a special permit.

items.definitionEn: a race combining swimming, cycling and running
items.example: The triathlon starts with a 750-metre swim in the lake.

items.definitionEn: a contest of five events, in the modern form including fencing and riding
items.example: The modern pentathlon still includes a show-jumping round.

items.definitionEn: a sport of lifting a loaded bar from the ground to above the head
items.example: Weightlifting at junior level is carefully supervised.

items.definitionEn: the sport of shooting arrows at a target with a bow
items.example: Archery requires a quiet hand and a lot of patience.

items.definitionEn: a combat sport using a foil, épée or sabre
items.example: Fencing masks protect the face from a stray blade.

items.definitionEn: the sport of racing boats that are moved with oars
items.example: Rowing on the river starts at dawn when the water is calm.

items.definitionEn: paddling a canoe, often as a race or on fast water
items.example: Canoeing on that stretch of river needs a helmet.

items.definitionEn: riding a board with a sail, using the wind on water
items.example: Windsurfing is easier on a lake than on a choppy sea.

items.definitionEn: swimming underwater with a tank of compressed air
items.example: Scuba diving around the wreck is only for certified divers.

items.definitionEn: climbing natural rock faces using hands, feet and safety gear
items.example: Indoor walls are a safer way to start rock climbing.

items.definitionEn: climbing high mountains, often with ice, snow and altitude
items.example: Mountaineering in the Tatras in winter needs avalanche training.

items.definitionEn: climbing short, difficult routes without a rope, using crash mats
items.example: Bouldering builds finger strength faster than long routes.

items.definitionEn: moving through a city or course by jumping, climbing and vaulting
items.example: Parkour in the shopping centre is against the rules.

items.definitionEn: ice skating that combines jumps, spins and dance steps
items.example: Figure skating scores both technical elements and artistic impression.

items.definitionEn: a winter sport combining cross-country skiing and rifle shooting
items.example: A missed target in the biathlon means extra penalty loops.

items.definitionEn: skiing down a ramp and jumping as far as possible
items.example: Ski jumping in Zakopane draws huge television audiences in Poland.

items.definitionEn: a sport on ice in which teams slide stones towards a target
items.example: Curling looks gentle until you try to sweep the ice at full speed.

items.definitionEn: a team ball game played in a pool, similar to handball in water
items.example: Water polo players need huge lung capacity and thick skin.

items.definitionEn: a sport in which swimmers perform a routine of movements to music
items.example: Synchronised swimming looks graceful but requires intense strength.

items.definitionEn: finding your way across country with a map and compass against the clock
items.example: Orienteering in the forest is harder when the paths look the same.

items.definitionEn: a riding event in which horse and rider jump a course of fences
items.example: A pole down in show jumping adds four faults to the score.

items.definitionEn: a cue sport played with 21 balls on a large table, popular in Britain
items.example: A maximum break in snooker is 147 points.

items.definitionEn: a team game similar to basketball, widely played in British schools
items.example: Netball is still more common than basketball in many girls' PE lessons.

items.definitionEn: a team game played with sticks and a ball on grass or artificial turf
items.example: Field hockey at this level is extremely fast and physical.

items.definitionEn: a 15-a-side rugby code with scrums, lineouts and tries worth five points
items.example: Rugby union at school is optional because of the injury risk.

items.definitionEn: a large sports ground with seats around the playing area
items.example: The new stadium holds forty thousand spectators.

items.definitionEn: the marked grass or turf area where football or rugby is played
items.example: Heavy rain left the pitch unfit for a Friday night fixture.

items.definitionEn: the marked area for tennis, basketball, volleyball or squash
items.example: We booked an indoor court because the wind was too strong.

items.definitionEn: the oval running surface used for track events
items.example: Six schools shared the athletics track on Wednesday afternoon.

items.definitionEn: a large indoor venue for sport or entertainment
items.example: The basketball final was played in a packed indoor arena.

items.definitionEn: a track, often banked, designed for cycle racing
items.example: The national velodrome is open to amateur clubs on Sunday mornings.

items.definitionEn: an ice surface for skating, ice hockey or curling
items.example: The ice rink closes in April and becomes a concert hall.

items.definitionEn: a prepared hillside used for skiing or snowboarding
items.example: The ski slope is floodlit until nine in the evening.

items.definitionEn: an area of land with numbered holes for playing golf
items.example: The municipal golf course is cheaper than the private club.

items.definitionEn: an indoor hall marked for several sports, often at a school
items.example: PE moves to the sports hall when the field is frozen.

items.definitionEn: a room where players change clothes before and after sport
items.example: Leave boots outside the changing room so the floor stays dry.

items.definitionEn: the shelter beside the pitch where the coach and substitutes sit
items.example: The manager stayed in the dugout until the equaliser.

items.definitionEn: the main, often covered, stand with the best seats
items.example: Season-ticket holders sit in the grandstand above the halfway line.

items.definitionEn: powerful lights that allow sport to be played after dark
items.example: The floodlights failed, so the second half was delayed.

items.definitionEn: a place designed for sport, such as a stadium, pool or hall
items.example: Every sports venue at the championships is accessible by tram.

items.definitionEn: a place with equipment for physical training
items.example: The gym is packed after work, so she trains at seven in the morning.

items.definitionEn: the strung implement used to hit the ball or shuttlecock
items.example: A broken string in her racket cost her the second set.

items.definitionEn: a hard hat that protects the head in cycling, skating or riding
items.example: A cycle helmet is compulsory in this race series.

items.definitionEn: guards worn on the lower legs, especially in football
items.example: The referee will not let you play without shin pads.

items.definitionEn: a plastic guard worn in the mouth to protect the teeth
items.example: Rugby players must wear a gumshield in every match.

items.definitionEn: protective glasses for swimming, skiing or cycling
items.example: Anti-fog goggles make the last length of the race easier.

items.definitionEn: a close-fitting rubber suit that keeps you warm in cold water
items.example: A winter wetsuit is essential for open-water swimming in March.

items.definitionEn: comfortable sports shoes for running or the gym
items.example: Do not wear fashion trainers on the indoor athletics track.

items.definitionEn: studded shoes designed for football or rugby on grass
items.example: Muddy football boots are not allowed in the school corridor.

items.definitionEn: running shoes with metal points for grip on a track
items.example: Borrow a pair of spikes if you are running the 400 metres.

items.definitionEn: a watch used to measure exact times in training or races
items.example: The coach clicked the stopwatch as she crossed the line.

items.definitionEn: a board that displays the score and sometimes the time
items.example: The scoreboard still showed 0–0 after forty minutes.

items.definitionEn: the two upright posts, and usually a bar, that form a goal
items.example: The shot hit the goalposts and bounced back into play.

items.definitionEn: the feathered or plastic object hit in badminton
items.example: A slow shuttlecock is easier for beginners to control.

items.definitionEn: the hard rubber disc used in ice hockey
items.example: The puck went in off a skate and the goal stood.

items.definitionEn: a long bar with weights at each end, used for lifting
items.example: Never lift a loaded barbell without a spotter.

items.definitionEn: short bars with weights, held in each hand
items.example: Start with light dumbbells until your technique is clean.

items.definitionEn: a machine with a moving belt that you run or walk on
items.example: Twenty minutes on the treadmill is her recovery session.

items.definitionEn: straps worn around the body and attached to a rope for safety
items.example: Check your harness twice before you leave the ground.

items.definitionEn: a long pole with a blade, used to row a boat
items.example: She snapped an oar in the last 200 metres of the race.

items.definitionEn: poles used for balance and push on skis
items.example: Adjust the straps on your ski poles before the first descent.

items.definitionEn: a scheduled match in a competition
items.example: Saturday's fixture was postponed because of a frozen pitch.

items.definitionEn: a series of games that continue until there is a winner
items.example: The junior tennis tournament lasts four days.

items.definitionEn: a competition to decide the best team or player in a sport
items.example: She won the national swimming championship in the 200 metres.

items.definitionEn: an early stage that decides who reaches the main competition
items.example: He failed to get through the qualifying round by two seconds.

items.definitionEn: a group of clubs that play one another over a season
items.example: Our club was promoted to a higher league last May.

items.definitionEn: a match in a knockout cup competition
items.example: A cup tie against a Premier League side is a huge occasion.

items.definitionEn: a match whose winner reaches the last four
items.example: They have never gone beyond the quarter-final of this event.

items.definitionEn: a match whose winner goes through to the final
items.example: A late penalty sent them out in the semi-final.

items.definitionEn: an extra match or series to decide promotion, qualification or a title
items.example: The play-off will be over two legs, home and away.

items.definitionEn: a match between two clubs from the same city or region
items.example: The Kraków derby always sells out within hours.

items.definitionEn: a match that does not count in a league or cup
items.example: The friendly against Wales is a chance to try a new formation.

items.definitionEn: additional playing time when a knockout match is still a draw
items.example: They scored two minutes into extra time.

items.definitionEn: taking turns at penalties to decide a drawn knockout match
items.example: We lost on a penalty shoot-out after a goalless draw.

items.definitionEn: the world's largest multi-sport event, held every four years
items.example: Hosting the Olympic Games can transform a city's transport.

items.definitionEn: the major international multi-sport event for athletes with disabilities
items.example: Coverage of the Paralympic Games is far better than a decade ago.

items.definitionEn: one of the four major tennis tournaments, or winning all four in a year
items.example: Winning a Grand Slam is still the peak of a tennis career.

items.definitionEn: the best official result ever achieved in an event
items.example: The world record in the marathon has fallen several times this decade.

items.definitionEn: the part of a tournament in which losing means elimination
items.example: Two draws in the group still put them into the knockout stage.

items.definitionEn: the opening round in which teams play in small groups
items.example: A defeat in the group stage does not always mean going home.

items.definitionEn: the official show that starts a major championship or Games
items.example: The opening ceremony featured dancers from every host region.

items.definitionEn: the official presentation of medals after an event
items.example: Tears at the medal ceremony are part of the television ritual.

items.definitionEn: a highly ranked competitor given a favourable place in the draw
items.example: A seeded player can still go out in the first round on a bad day.

items.definitionEn: an early race that decides who reaches the next round
items.example: She won her heat comfortably and saved energy for the final.

items.definitionEn: the first kick that starts a football match; the scheduled start time
items.example: Kick-off has been moved to midday because of the heat.

items.definitionEn: the official who controls a football, rugby or boxing contest
items.example: The referee added five minutes for time-wasting.

items.definitionEn: the official who controls tennis, cricket, volleyball or badminton
items.example: The umpire overruled the line judge after a challenge.

items.definitionEn: an official who helps the referee, especially with offside and throw-ins
items.example: The assistant referee raised the flag a moment too late.

items.definitionEn: a player who comes on in place of a teammate
items.example: The substitute scored with his first touch of the ball.

items.definitionEn: a person who watches a sports event in person
items.example: Every spectator was asked not to use a laser pointer.

items.definitionEn: a person who causes violence or damage in connection with sport
items.example: A known hooligan was banned from every ground in the league.

items.definitionEn: a person who trains a team or athlete
items.example: The coach changed the formation at half-time.

items.definitionEn: the person in charge of a football club's team affairs
items.example: The manager refused to criticise the referee after the defeat.

items.definitionEn: the player who leads the team on the field
items.example: The captain asked the umpire to check the ball.

items.definitionEn: the player whose job is to stop the ball going into the goal
items.example: The goalkeeper saved the last penalty of the shoot-out.

items.definitionEn: a forward whose main job is to score goals
items.example: The young striker has eight goals in ten league matches.

items.definitionEn: a player whose main job is to stop the other team scoring
items.example: The defender cleared the ball off the line.

items.definitionEn: a player who links defence and attack in the middle of the pitch
items.example: The midfielder covered more ground than anyone else on the field.

items.definitionEn: a person who describes a match live on television or radio
items.example: The sports commentator apologised for shouting during the goal.

items.definitionEn: a former player or expert who analyses sport on television
items.example: The studio pundit predicted a draw and was proved wrong.

items.definitionEn: a person who watches players to find talent for a club
items.example: A scout from a German club sat in the stand with a notebook.

items.definitionEn: a physiotherapist who treats sports injuries
items.example: The physio signalled that the winger could not continue.

items.definitionEn: a person who helps with safety and crowd control at a venue
items.example: A steward asked him to take off the large flag on a pole.

items.definitionEn: a person who regularly follows and backs a particular team
items.example: The away supporter was held in the station for an hour after the match.

items.definitionEn: a person who represents an athlete in contracts and transfers
items.example: The sports agent negotiated a clause about image rights.

items.definitionEn: a person who plays sport without being paid as a professional
items.example: He remains an amateur while he finishes university.

items.definitionEn: a person who is paid to play sport as their job
items.example: Very few junior players become a full-time professional.

items.definitionEn: the ability to keep exercising hard for a long time
items.example: Long Sunday runs are how she builds stamina for the marathon.

items.definitionEn: your own fastest or best result in an event
items.example: She ran a personal best but still finished fourth.

items.definitionEn: gentle exercise done before a hard session or match
items.example: A proper warm-up reduces the risk of a pulled muscle.

items.definitionEn: gentle exercise after sport so the body recovers gradually
items.example: Skip the cool-down and you will be stiff tomorrow.

items.definitionEn: a session of short exercises done one after another at stations
items.example: Circuit training twice a week improved his general fitness.

items.definitionEn: alternating bursts of hard effort with recovery periods
items.example: Interval training on the track is tougher than a steady jog.

items.definitionEn: exercise using weights to build strength
items.example: Sprinters use weight training to improve their start.

items.definitionEn: the ability to keep going in long-lasting physical effort
items.example: Cycling to school every day builds endurance without a gym.

items.definitionEn: the ability to change direction quickly and under control
items.example: Ladder drills are meant to improve agility, not just look busy.

items.definitionEn: the ability to use different parts of the body together smoothly
items.example: Juggling tennis balls can actually help hand-eye coordination.

items.definitionEn: how far your joints and muscles can stretch
items.example: Gymnasts need exceptional flexibility in the spine and hips.

items.definitionEn: the process of the body repairing itself after training
items.example: Sleep is a bigger part of recovery than any protein bar.

items.definitionEn: training so hard or so often that performance and health get worse
items.example: Irritability and a resting pulse that will not drop can signal overtraining.

items.definitionEn: eating extra carbohydrates before a long event to store energy
items.example: Carbohydrate loading is useful before a marathon, not before a 100-metre sprint.

items.definitionEn: a drink with caffeine and sugar, marketed to boost alertness or performance
items.example: An energy drink is not a substitute for water during training.

items.definitionEn: keeping enough fluid in the body during exercise
items.example: Hydration matters more in a long match than in a short race.

items.definitionEn: reducing training load shortly before a competition so you arrive fresh
items.example: Tapering in the last ten days made her legs feel light on race morning.

items.definitionEn: doing a different sport to support your main one and reduce injury
items.example: Swimming is her cross-training on days when her knees hurt.

items.definitionEn: a coach who designs and supervises exercise for an individual
items.example: A personal trainer corrected her squat before it damaged her back.

items.definitionEn: a period when athletes live and train together, often away from home
items.example: The national team holds a training camp in Spain every January.

items.definitionEn: the training period before the competitive season starts
items.example: Pre-season is when fitness is rebuilt after the summer break.

items.definitionEn: the period when there is no official competition
items.example: In the off-season he works on strength rather than match fitness.

items.definitionEn: the highest level of condition an athlete can reach for a target event
items.example: She timed her peak fitness for the Olympic trials, not the winter races.

items.definitionEn: illegally boosting performance by manipulating blood or red cells
items.example: Blood doping is harder to detect than some tablets, but it is still cheating.

items.definitionEn: using banned substances or methods to improve sporting results
items.example: Doping scandals have damaged public trust in cycling.

items.definitionEn: illegally arranging the result or events of a match, often for betting
items.example: Three players were banned for life after a match-fixing inquiry.

items.definitionEn: the principle that women and men should receive comparable pay and prizes
items.example: The campaign for equal pay in sport grew after the World Cup win.

items.definitionEn: fair, respectful behaviour towards opponents and officials
items.example: Lending a spare wheel to a rival is still remembered as sportsmanship.

items.definitionEn: money given to a student because of athletic ability
items.example: A sports scholarship allowed him to train and study at the same time.

items.definitionEn: playing by the rules and showing respect, even when it costs you
items.example: Kicking the ball out when a player is down is basic fair play.

items.definitionEn: a drug or chemical that athletes are not allowed to use
items.example: Even a cold remedy can contain a banned substance.

items.definitionEn: a drug taken to improve strength, speed, endurance or recovery
items.example: A performance-enhancing drug can destroy a career after one positive test.

items.definitionEn: an official check of blood or urine for banned substances
items.example: Athletes can be asked for a drug test at home, not only after races.

items.definitionEn: a punishment that stops someone competing for the rest of their life
items.example: Match officials received a life ban after the bribery case.

items.definitionEn: organised or spontaneous violence by fans around sports events
items.example: Hooliganism in the 1980s led to fences and ID schemes.

items.definitionEn: unfair treatment or abuse of people because of race in a sporting context
items.example: Players walked off the pitch in protest against racism in sport.

items.definitionEn: a brain injury from a blow to the head, common in contact sport
items.example: Any suspicion of concussion means the player must leave the field.

items.definitionEn: the process of recovering fitness and skill after injury
items.example: Rehabilitation after the knee operation lasted nine months.

items.definitionEn: video technology that helps football referees review key decisions
items.example: VAR disallowed the goal for a narrow offside.

items.definitionEn: a caution from the referee for unsporting behaviour or a foul
items.example: A second yellow card in the tournament means a one-match ban.

items.definitionEn: a sending-off, leaving the team with one fewer player
items.example: A red card in the first half made the comeback almost impossible.

items.definitionEn: the act of dismissing a player from the match
items.example: The sending-off was for violent conduct, not a tactical foul.

items.definitionEn: using legal but unsporting tricks to gain an advantage
items.example: Time-wasting is gamesmanship, not the same as breaking the rules.

items.definitionEn: deliberately slowing the game to protect a lead
items.example: The referee booked the goalkeeper for obvious time-wasting.

items.definitionEn: pretending to be fouled in order to win a free kick or penalty
items.example: Diving in the box can now be punished with a yellow card.

items.definitionEn: the money one club pays another to sign a player under contract
items.example: The transfer fee broke the club's previous record.

items.definitionEn: local, amateur sport that develops participation rather than elite results
items.example: Cuts to playing fields hurt grassroots sport more than the professional game.

items.definitionEn: sport at the highest competitive level, usually professional
items.example: Funding for elite sport is easier to justify when medals come in.

items.definitionEn: a sudden feeling of excitement caused by danger or intense effort
items.example: The adrenaline rush after a bungee jump lasts only a minute.

items.definitionEn: jumping from an aircraft and falling before opening a parachute
items.example: Tandem skydiving is how most beginners make a first jump.

items.definitionEn: riding an inflatable raft down fast, rough river water
items.example: White-water rafting on that river is closed when the level is too high.

items.definitionEn: jumping from a height with an elastic cord attached to the body
items.example: Bungee jumping from the bridge is banned in high wind.

items.definitionEn: parachuting from a fixed object such as a cliff or building
items.example: Base jumping is illegal in many national parks.

items.definitionEn: paid something to play, but not enough to live on as a full-time job
items.example: Most players in the third division are still semi-professional.

items.definitionEn: the club's main senior side, not the reserves or youth team
items.example: He trained with the first team for two weeks before debuting.

items.definitionEn: a club's system for training talented young players
items.example: Leaving the youth academy at sixteen is a huge risk.

items.definitionEn: basketball played in sports wheelchairs, including at Paralympic level
items.example: Wheelchair basketball is one of the fastest Paralympic team sports.

items.definitionEn: sport organised for athletes with disabilities at elite international level
items.example: Classification is a constant debate in Paralympic sport.

items.definitionEn: a ticket that covers all of a team's home matches in a season
items.example: A season ticket in the main stand costs more than a holiday.

items.definitionEn: the benefit a team gets from playing at its own ground
items.example: Noise from the home crowd is part of home advantage.

items.definitionEn: a match played at the opponent's ground
items.example: The away fixture in Gdańsk means a six-hour bus trip.

items.definitionEn: the ranking of clubs by points during a league season
items.example: Goal difference could decide the league table on the last day.

items.definitionEn: three goals scored by the same player in one match
items.example: Her hat-trick came from a header, a tap-in and a penalty.

items.definitionEn: a goal accidentally scored in your own team's net
items.example: An own goal in the ninety-fourth minute ended the unbeaten run.

items.definitionEn: a rule that a player is too far forward when the ball is played
items.example: The goal was ruled out for offside after a VAR review.

items.definitionEn: the study and practice of the mental side of sporting performance
items.example: Sports psychology helped him deal with the fear of a second injury.

items.definitionEn: physical damage caused by training or competition
items.example: A sports injury at eighteen ended her hopes of a professional contract.

items.definitionEn: making sport open and fair for people of different abilities, genders and backgrounds
items.example: Inclusion in sport means ramps at the pool, not only slogans on shirts.
